summary:
Moonrizon is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates, built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. The user picks a site on an interactive 3D Moon (a historic landing site, a 2022 Artemis III candidate region near the south pole, or any custom coordinates), then sets a date and a time period. The backend builds the real local horizon from NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data and checks Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons against it. From this it works out when the site has sunlight, when Earth is in view for direct-to-Earth communication, and when both are available at once.

The results appear on the globe, in a 360° horizon panorama, on timelines and in side-by-side reports. Users can filter sites by mission requirements and estimate solar energy with their own panel, load and battery settings.

This matters because south-pole terrain makes light and communication change sharply over short distances. Landing dates for commercial missions also slip often. NASA QuickMap, Moon Trek and Horizons hold the data but are complex to use. Moonrizon puts that data in one place, with documented sources, so planners, educators and the public can quickly re-check a site or a new date.
details:
What it does and how it works

Moonrizon is a web app that shows how sunlight and the line of sight to Earth change at a lunar location over time. The user starts on an interactive 3D Moon and picks a site from our catalog or enters any coordinates. The catalog has the 13 candidate regions NASA announced for Artemis III in 2022 and 9 documented landing sites. The user then sets a start date in UTC and how long to analyze.

The backend runs the calculation in two background jobs:

  1. Terrain analysis. It loads NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data and builds the real local horizon all the way around the observer. This includes near and distant terrain and the Moon’s curvature. It also fits the local slope over a 100 m circle.
  2. Sun and Earth visibility. It requests Sun and Earth positions for that exact place from NASA/JPL Horizons and compares them with the horizon. It doesn’t treat the Sun as a single point: it works out what fraction of the solar disc is above the terrain. From this it finds when the site has sunlight, when Earth is in view for direct-to-Earth communication, and when both happen at once. It also gives how long each break lasts.

The results appear in linked views:

  • the 3D globe;
  • a 360° horizon panorama with the paths of the Sun and Earth;
  • a timeline of visibility windows;
  • reports.

Users can compare up to four points side by side or run a comparison across the whole catalog.

Benefits

  • One place to answer “will this site have light and a link to Earth on this date?” instead of switching between several expert tools.
  • Fast re-checks when a launch date slips, which happens often for commercial lunar missions.
  • Mission requirements the user can edit: minimum sunlight, Earth visibility and overlap, longest allowed break, maximum slope and minimum data resolution. Sites that fail a requirement are excluded. Sites that pass are ranked by trade-offs (Pareto fronts) instead of one opaque score.
  • An optional solar energy estimate with the user’s own panel, load and battery settings.
  • A demo mode with clearly labeled example data, for classrooms and the public.

Intended impact

We want to make lunar landing-site reasoning accessible to mission planners doing early studies, to educators, and to anyone curious about the Moon’s south pole. That region has long shadows, low Sun angles and Earth sitting near the horizon, so conditions change sharply over short distances and from one week to the next. Moonrizon makes those effects visible and easy to compare.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, CesiumJS.
  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, Shapely, pytest.
  • Storage: no database. Data lives in files: GeoTIFF, Parquet, GeoJSON and JSON, cached on disk with provenance records.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose and nginx. The interface is generated from the backend’s OpenAPI schema.
  • Data: NASA Moon Trek (region outlines, catalogs, imagery), NASA PDS/PGDA LRO-LOLA (elevation), NASA/JPL Horizons (Sun and Earth positions), LROC images (independent shadow checks), NASA QuickMap (manual reference).
  • Hardware: standard laptops only.
  • AI-assisted development: ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Cursor.

What makes it creative

  • It uses the real terrain horizon in every direction instead of a flat horizon, and treats the Sun as a disc that can be partly hidden.
  • It turns expert tools into a few linked views where you can see the Sun set behind a specific ridge.
  • It ranks sites by trade-offs instead of naming a single “best site”.
  • It is honest about data: a missing value stays unknown, with a reason, and is never assumed to be good. A data gap is kept separate from a real sunset or Earthset.

Factors we considered

  • No atmosphere, so no refraction. The horizon comes only from terrain and the Moon’s curvature.
  • Libration. Earth’s position in the lunar sky changes, which matters most near the poles. We take observer-specific positions from Horizons instead of approximating them.
  • Observer height. Our command-line engine uses 2 m above the ground, which is a team choice. The web API also accepts other heights.
  • Data sources and limits. Every source is recorded with its version and checksum. We never resample data to look more detailed than it is. A region’s center is one point, not an assessment of the whole region.
  • Validation and scope. The numerical checks passed. The comparison with real LROC images is not finished. Results only describe geometry: they don’t establish landing safety, power or radio performance.
  • Accessibility. The app works for both experts and newcomers, with plain metrics, visual timelines and a demo mode.
